finding.claim: GET /users has no authentication or tenant binding; the org filter is taken directly from the client, so any unauthenticated caller can list users of any org.
finding.sink: SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE org = $1 returned as JSON (db.js:9-10)

trace.note: GET /users route registered with no auth middleware in this file
req.query.org passed as the tenant scope parameter; not tied to any session, token or user identity
all matching id and name rows returned to the caller

finding.guards_checked: Query is parameterized ($1), so no SQL injection. No auth or tenant check visible in this file. req.pg is injected externally, so an upstream auth layer could not be confirmed from this code; the finding holds unless one exists.

verdict.guard_found: none. db.js:8 registers GET /users directly on the app with no middleware, and no app.use() or auth wrapper appears anywhere in db.js. db.js:9 passes req.query.org straight into the query as $1, which is parameterized and so blocks SQL injection but not the authorization gap. db.js:10 returns the rows as JSON. The directory holds only db.js, and nothing in it sets req.pg or adds auth.
verdict.reason: The route is registered without auth at db.js:8, the org filter comes from the client at db.js:9, and the rows are returned unfiltered at db.js:10, so an anonymous caller can list users of any org. This is confirmed against the code available, but the claim assumes db.js is the whole deployed app; a gateway outside this directory could still add auth.
